statement: In a US national survey of adults interviewed in 2001–2002 and again in 2004–2005 (the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions; 34,653 people at both interviews), the estimated chance of ever becoming dependent was well under one in two for people who had used cannabis, cocaine or alcohol, and about two in three for people who had ever smoked a full cigarette. Among people who had ever used each substance (stated as 7,389 for cannabis, 2,259 for cocaine or crack, 28,907 for alcohol and 15,918 for nicotine), the estimated probability of meeting DSM-IV criteria for dependence at some time in life was 8.9% for cannabis, 20.9% for cocaine, 22.7% for alcohol and 67.5% for nicotine; within 10 years of first use it was 5.9%, 14.8%, 11.0% and 15.6%, and within the first year almost 2% for cannabis, alcohol and nicotine and 7.1% for cocaine. Among the people who became dependent, half had done so within about 4 years of first using cocaine, 5 years for cannabis, 13 for alcohol and 27 for nicotine (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011). Dependence meant three or more of seven DSM-IV criteria within the same 12 months (signs such as tolerance, withdrawal, using more than intended or failing to stop after resolving to; Heyman, 2013), diagnosed by computer from answers to a structured interview; use meant a first full cigarette, at least one drink not counting sips, or any use of cannabis or of cocaine or crack. These are survey reports: everything rests on what people said, without tests, and on ages they recalled, sometimes decades later; the lifetime figures are projections from survival curves that join younger and older people's histories, and no interval is given for any of them; and the survey left out people living in institutions such as prisons, who the authors say are more likely to have a dependence diagnosis, and, at the second interview, people who had died, been deported, become too impaired to take part or gone on active military duty, so the figures are probably somewhat too low (editors' inference). In the adjusted models, dependence was more likely among people with a mood, anxiety or personality disorder or with dependence on another substance (hazard ratios 1.42 to 4.14), associations that cannot show cause; in the same models neither education nor income predicted dependence, although lower individual income went with it before adjustment (hazard ratios up to 2.77 for cannabis and 2.76 for cocaine, lowest against highest income band) and income could not be modelled as changing over time. Carl Hart, a Columbia University professor of psychology and psychiatry who studies drug effects in people, argues in a one-page opinion piece, without numbers or sources, that the vast majority of people who use cocaine and other recreational drugs never become addicted and that among the relatively few who do, co-occurring psychiatric disorders and socioeconomic factors account for a substantial share (Hart, 2017); in a second opinion piece he states that 70% to 90% of people who use even heroin or methamphetamine do not meet criteria for a substance use disorder, citing only his own book and giving no survey, year or definition (Hart, 2020). The survey's estimates fit his first statement for cannabis, cocaine and alcohol but not for nicotine, and no survey read here gives a figure for heroin or methamphetamine, so his range cannot be checked against them (editors' comparison). An earlier US survey (1990–1992), whose figures count dependence by the time of the interview rather than over a projected lifetime and include heroin, is described in the answer on how many people who use cannabis become dependent; how often people stop meeting the criteria is the answer on recovery from drug or alcohol problems. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: Do most people who try drugs get addicted? Not for most drugs. In a large US survey from 2001 to 2005, about 9 in 100 people who had ever used cannabis, 21 in 100 who had used cocaine and 23 in 100 who had used alcohol were expected to become dependent at some point in their lives. Tobacco was the exception: about 68 in 100 people who had smoked a full cigarette. For cannabis and cocaine, half of those who became dependent did so within about 4 to 5 years of first use; for alcohol it was 13 years, for tobacco 27. Dependence meant at least 3 of 7 signs within the same year, such as needing more for the same effect, withdrawal, or not managing to stop. It was more common in people with depression, an anxiety disorder or another dependence, a link rather than proof of a cause. The figures rest on people's own answers and memories, and the survey left out people in prisons and people who had died, so the real figures may be somewhat higher. The researcher Carl Hart argues that most people who use drugs never become addicted, but gives no data of his own; the survey fits that for cannabis, cocaine and alcohol, not for tobacco, and has no figures for heroin or meth.
population: US civilian adults living in households and group quarters, interviewed in 2001–2002 and again in 2004–2005 (34,653 at both interviews; Black and Hispanic people and adults aged 18 to 24 oversampled; estimates weighted to the US population), in the subsamples who had ever used each substance (stated as 15,918 for nicotine, 28,907 for alcohol, 7,389 for cannabis and 2,259 for cocaine or crack)
exposure: Ever having used the substance (a first full cigarette; at least one drink, not counting small tastes or sips; any cannabis; any cocaine or crack), from the recalled age of first use
comparator: None for the probabilities (descriptive); for the predictors, people who had used the substance without the characteristic
outcome: Meeting DSM-IV criteria for dependence (three or more of seven within 12 months) at some time after first use, diagnosed by computer from a structured interview (AUDADIS-IV) with recalled ages of onset; cumulative probability by years since first use (actuarial survival estimates), and predictors as hazard ratios
magnitude: Lopez-Quintero et al. (2011), actuarial cumulative probability of DSM-IV dependence among people who had ever used each substance (no intervals given): lifetime nicotine 67.5%, alcohol 22.7%, cocaine 20.9%, cannabis 8.9%; 10 years after first use 15.6%, 11.0%, 14.8%, 5.9%; first year almost 2.0% (nicotine, alcohol, cannabis) and 7.1% (cocaine); half of the cases of dependence about 27, 13, 5 and 4 years after first use (a median among the people who became dependent). Stated subsamples 15,918, 28,907, 7,389 and 2,259 (the rows of Tables 1 and 2 add to 16,053, 29,160, 7,409 and 2,263). Adjusted hazard ratios (Table 4), nicotine / alcohol / cannabis / cocaine: mood disorder 1.62 / 2.29 / 2.69 / 2.58; anxiety disorder 1.96 / 1.98 / 2.31 / not retained; personality disorder 1.42 / 1.64 / 2.3 / 1.99; dependence on another of the four substances 1.44 to 4.14. Unadjusted, lowest against highest individual income (Table 3): 1.39 / 1.23 / 2.77 / 2.76. Hart (2017, 2020): opinion pieces with no data; the range he states for heroin and methamphetamine is not used as a figure.

evidence.extracted: NESARC: US civilian non-institutionalized adults in households and group quarters, with Black and Hispanic people and adults aged 18 to 24 oversampled; 43,093 interviewed at Wave 1 and 34,653 re-interviewed at Wave 2 (2004–2005); people who had died (1,403), been deported or become mentally or physically impaired (781) or were on active military duty (950) were not eligible at Wave 2; weights adjust for non-response. Analyses in the people who had ever used each substance (15,918 nicotine, 28,907 alcohol, 7,389 cannabis, 2,259 cocaine), use meaning a first full cigarette, at least one drink not counting small tastes or sips, or any cannabis or cocaine or crack. DSM-IV dependence (3 or more of 7 criteria within a 12-month period) produced by computer algorithms from the AUDADIS-IV structured interview, test-retest kappa 0.54 to 0.91 for substance use disorder diagnoses.

risk_of_bias.note: Not downgraded for the claim as worded (card sc_lopez_quintero_2011: JBI moderate; its printed pages and funding were checked against the version of record in 734_checks.json). A national probability sample with weights for non-response and one structured interview for every substance; but everything is self-reported, ages of first use and of dependence were recalled, sometimes decades later, the lifetime figures are actuarial projections without intervals, and people in institutions, and people who died, were deported, became impaired or went on military duty before the second interview, were not included. These limits would mostly lower the figures, which the statement gives as probably somewhat too low, and could not plausibly make dependence the usual outcome for cannabis, cocaine or alcohol. The nicotine lifetime figure and the timing figures (within 10 years, within the first year, the medians) rest most on the projection and on recalled ages; on their own they would be rated down one level, to very low, as in the answer on how many people who use cannabis become dependent. The predictors come from stepwise models whose covariates differ between substances, and are worded as associations.

inconsistency.note: One survey. The authors say its decade figures agree with an earlier national survey (Wagner & Anthony, 2002, not read), and its cannabis figure is close to that of the 1990–1992 survey described in the answer on cannabis dependence.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: US household adults interviewed in 2001–2005, DSM-IV dependence on four substances, use defined as a first cigarette, drink or use; the statement says no figure here covers heroin or methamphetamine and names the measure.

imprecision.note: No interval is printed for any cumulative probability, but the estimates rest on 2,259 to 28,907 people who had used each substance, with 376 to 7,320 dependence cases in the models.

publication_bias.note: Not applicable to a national survey analysis.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive claim (cumulative probabilities in a survey population): starts low and is never upgraded (METHODS 6.3); not downgraded (see the domain notes), so low. Strict reading: the nicotine lifetime projection and the timing figures alone would be very low (risk of bias -1). Status single study: one survey, whose two waves are one study; the earlier national surveys mentioned are not anchored here and are not counted. Hart's two opinion pieces (narrative-review design on their cards) give no data and are used only for what he argues, beside the survey's figures, never as the source of a number; they do not enter the rating, and the comparison of his statements with the survey is the editors'. Heyman (2013) is used only for examples of the DSM-IV criteria. The predictors are associations from stepwise models and do not enter the rating of the probabilities.

verification.flag_note: Theme 27 ('How fast do people get hooked, and can anyone use drugs without losing control?'); question 1 of reader 752 in round pdf-2026-11-26. Rests on one survey, read in the version of record (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011); its supplementary tables (characteristics of the people who became dependent) were not on file. No survey read here gives a figure for heroin, methamphetamine or other drugs: Anthony et al. (1994), already on the site in the answers on cannabis and stimulant dependence, gives 1990–1992 figures including heroin and could be added by the editor; Wagner & Anthony (2002), which the authors say their decade figures agree with, was not read. Hart (2017, 2020) are opinion pieces with no data, cited only for what he argues; his 70% to 90% is cited to his 2013 book (High Price), not read. The measure is DSM-IV dependence, not today's use-disorder diagnosis (the difference is in the answer on cannabis dependence). The card's statement that the probabilities are 'likely underestimated' is an inference: the paper says only that people in institutions, who were excluded, more often have a dependence diagnosis.
